title: How the browser is built and looks

entities.title: One HTML file, no build
entities.summary: The page is a single file that runs in the reader's browser; the Worker serves it as it is.
entities.context: The browser has to be easy to host, copy and trust with a private repository.
entities.decision: Markup, styles, script and icons are in index.html. It talks to the repository's host straight from the browser, and loads only dagre, the typefaces and, on first entry to Cyberspace, three.js from jsDelivr. The Worker at cyberspace-explorer.com imports the file as text and serves it unchanged; it adds GitHub sign-in, and nothing the page needs to work.
entities.rationale: There is nothing to build, any static host can serve it, and a reader who doesn't sign in gives no server their repository or token.
entities.details: Earlier the decision was "no server" too. The Worker, with its sign-in, came later ([its decisions](worker/.dev/decisions.json)); served as a plain file the page still works, with pasted tokens.

entities.title: The page draws its own diagrams
entities.summary: dagre places parts; the page draws everything.
entities.context: Each kind of diagram reads best with its own shapes, and a general diagramming library would set the look.
entities.decision: dagre 3.1.3 only positions parts and routes lines. Shapes, lines, arrowheads, labels and icons are SVG written by the page, one drawing per kind, sharing one layout and one renderer.
entities.rationale: The drawings look like one family and like the rest of the page, and only one library is needed.

entities.title: A survey sheet: cool paper and slate ink
entities.summary: The page's look is a surveyor's sheet.
entities.context: The page is read for long stretches and is mostly drawings and tables.
entities.decision: Light: paper #edf1f1, sheet #f8fafa, plates #ffffff, ink #1d2b33 with #56666e and #84949b for secondary and faint text, rules #c9d3d5. Dark: paper #10181d, sheet #152128, plates #1b2a32, ink #dce5e5. Drawings sit on the sheet with a small cross at every 24-unit grid point, and parts are white plates with a soft shadow in their kind's colour.
entities.rationale: Quiet surfaces let the one colour per kind carry the meaning.

entities.title: One colour per kind
entities.summary: Each kind of view has one colour, used everywhere that kind appears.
entities.context: A reader moves between ten kinds of view and needs to know at a glance which one they are in.
entities.decision: Component #2c6e8e, deployment #a26a14, class #527a31, state #8b4a8c, use case #bb5430, capability #4f58b0, feature #b0456f, operation #5b6a72, user journey #1f7f74, knowledge #7a5f36, each with a lighter value for dark mode. The colour marks the kind's icon, pips, tab underline, plate outlines and tints, card edges and the inspector.
entities.rationale: The kind is recognisable from any part of the page without reading.
entities.details: In Cyberspace the kind colour is an accent (decision space-gibson-look): towers are cyan glass whatever their kind, and the kind colour marks their edges, pads, labels, plates' rims and names, the frames and headings on their faces, and the floors of the folder tower and the skyline. Cyberspace uses the dark values, being always dark, whatever the theme switch says (decision theme-switch).

entities.title: Barlow in three widths
entities.summary: One type family, in three widths, with a system monospace.
entities.context: The page sets long names in narrow places: tree rows, plates, tabs, table headers.
entities.decision: Barlow (400, 500) for reading text at 16 px; Barlow Semi Condensed (500, 600) for labels, tabs, headings, the tree and inside drawings; Barlow Condensed (600, 700) for the brand, the landing headline and a folder's name, set large. Paths, IDs and symbols are in the system monospace.
entities.rationale: Condensed widths fit more of a name in a plate or a row while staying one family.

entities.title: Icons drawn for the page
entities.summary: Every icon is drawn for this page on a 24-unit grid.
entities.context: Icons mark kinds, groups and parts, and a part's icon should say what it is.
entities.decision: Strokes of 1.6 with round ends, and one tinted shape per glyph so each reads as a small solid object. A component's icon is chosen from its name (an engine gets a gear, a renderer a screen, a database a cylinder, and so on, with a cube when nothing matches); a deployment node's from its kind; a type's from its kind.
entities.rationale: The drawings say something before they are read, and the icons match the drawings.

entities.title: A folder shows one kind at a time
entities.summary: Tabs by kind, with all knowledge under one tab.
entities.context: A folder can have a dozen views and knowledge files, and drawings need room.
entities.decision: A tab per kind, in a fixed order; the open kind stays open from folder to folder. Every knowledge file shares one tab, grouped as the catalogue groups them.
entities.rationale: A reader sees one kind at full width, and following one kind through the tree keeps them on it.

entities.title: Every view is also tables
entities.summary: A drawing is a way in, not the only way.
entities.context: A drawing can fail to load, be too dense, or hide a detail.
entities.decision: Under each drawing a disclosure holds the view in full as tables: parts, relationships or transitions, related views and sources, with the file itself linked.
entities.rationale: Nothing a view says is only in a picture.

entities.title: One moment of motion
entities.summary: Opening a folder through a drawing is the page's one animation.
entities.context: Motion should say something.
entities.decision: The badged part grows into the page as its folder opens. Beyond that the page only pulses a part or flashes a record it has moved to, fades what is not lit and ticks while loading; all of it is off with reduced motion.
entities.rationale: The one movement explains where the reader has gone: into the part.

entities.title: In Cyberspace, motion takes the reader where they asked
entities.summary: Cyberspace's camera moves are motion beyond one-motion: they only take the reader where they asked to go, and reduced motion turns them all off.
entities.context: Decision one-motion allows the page one animation, the drill. Cyberspace needs camera moves: flying to a part, sliding a floor out of the folder tower, rising from the street back to the city.
entities.decision: In Cyberspace, motion only moves the camera, or a floor, to where the reader asked to go: flights between poses, a floor sliding out and back, and the fades that go with a change of scene. Nothing moves on its own. With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce every flight, slide and fade is instant; walking still moves, because the reader drives it. This amends one-motion; Flat keeps its one moment of motion.
entities.rationale: A move the reader asked for shows where they went, as the drill does in Flat; motion nobody asked for would only distract.
entities.details: Built (plan cyberspace-mode, steps city, selection, tower and street): the camera moves while the reader drags, scrolls, pinches or presses a key, and when the inspector they opened or closed changes the room left for the city, over 300 ms; a floor of the folder tower slides out and back over 450 ms when the reader pulls another out or slides it back; and the camera flies between the tower and a city (600 ms) when they enter a floor or go up with Esc, Back or Forward, the tower fading out or in over 200 ms. Each is at once with reduced motion, and input during a flight stops it where it is. The camera also flies from a city down to its street and back up (400 ms and 12 more a unit the eye travels, from 500 to 1200, on an arc), and the eye flies to where the reader clicks on the street's map; a plate under the walking eye is a step it eases onto over 150 ms. Walking itself moves only while the reader holds a key or drags, and it moves with reduced motion too, because the reader drives it. The camera flies between the skyline and a folder's tower (600 ms) as one fades out and the other in, and flies to another folder's building when the skyline's address changes. An unticked layer fades to the dim state over 200 ms before it goes, and a camera the reader hasn't moved fits to what stands over 300 ms when a layer comes or goes. Each is at once with reduced motion. Checked again in Chrome on 2026-11-15 (step 8), counting the animation frames asked for in the 1.6 s after each move: 36 to 148 with motion for tower to city, a selection's refit, city to street and back, city to tower, a floor sliding out, tower to skyline, building to building and skyline to tower; 2 for each with reduced motion. Since 2026-11-15, at the owner's request, the view turns toward a selection (docs/cyberspace-mode-spec.md, Camera and input, Looking at the selection): in a city the point the camera turns about glides to the part's middle, which comes to the centre of the room the inspector leaves, distance and angles kept, for as long as a flight over the distance; in the street the eye turns where it stands to face the part, for 250 ms and 3 more a degree, at most 700; in the tower the camera climbs to the floor selected. Keyboard focus moves the camera only to bring what it names just inside the room. Input stops a turn where it is; each is at once with reduced motion, and clearing the selection moves nothing.

entities.title: The address is the state
entities.summary: Once a repository is open, the address says what is shown.
entities.context: Links are how readers share what they see.
entities.decision: The repository is in ?url= and the place in it after #. The landing page's form only sets ?url=; there is no address field once a repository is open, and Choose another repository returns to the landing page.
entities.rationale: Every place can be linked to, and back and forward work.

entities.title: Tokens stay in the reader's browser, by scope
entities.summary: Each token is kept under the host and scope it is for.
entities.context: Readers have private repositories on several hosts and accounts, and must not leak a token to the wrong host.
entities.decision: Tokens are kept in sessionStorage, or localStorage when asked, under a scope; the narrowest scope around a repository wins. GitHub files are read from raw.githubusercontent.com without a token and through the API with one, because raw.githubusercontent.com turns away an Authorization header.
entities.rationale: No server holds a pasted token, and several accounts work side by side.
entities.details: A reader signed in with GitHub through the Worker uses that sign-in for GitHub instead, and the Worker holds that token ([token-off-the-page](worker/.dev/decisions.json)).

entities.title: A repository may keep all its views in .cyberspace-explorer
entities.summary: A .cyberspace-explorer folder at the root can hold what the .dev folders would, folder by folder.
entities.context: A .dev folder in every folder spreads views through the source tree, which some repositories would rather keep out of it.
entities.decision: foo/.dev/x.json and .cyberspace-explorer/foo/x.json mean the same, and .cyberspace-explorer/x.json is the root folder's x.json. If the root has a .cyberspace-explorer folder the page reads only that and does not look for .dev folders. A path written either way in a view finds the same view.
entities.rationale: One folder at the root holds every view, and a repository that has not moved is read as before.

entities.title: When the Cyberspace switch appears
entities.summary: Each step of Cyberspace is merged and deployed as it is built. The Flat / Cyberspace switch was to appear when step 7 was done; the owner had it shown on 2026-11-15, after step 6.
entities.context: Merging to main deploys to cyberspace-explorer.com, and the Worker has no preview URLs. Cyberspace is built in eight pull requests (plan cyberspace-mode).

options.title: Merge every step, the switch hidden until step 7
options.consequences: Small changes that never drift from main, and nothing half-built for readers. The changes to route() and select() reach readers before the launch, so every step checks the flat page again.

options.title: Merge every step, the switch shown from step 1
options.consequences: Readers find a mode that at first shows only a grid, and that lacks keyboard, reduced-motion and light-mode support until step 7.

options.title: One long-lived branch, merged once
options.consequences: Nothing reaches readers early, but the branch drifts while others change index.html, and one large merge is hard to review.

entities.decision: One pull request per step into main. The switch is built in step 1 and stays hidden until step 7 meets the recorded quality requirements: keyboard, reduced motion, light and dark, fallbacks. Until then only an address with ~space in it opens Cyberspace. On 2026-11-15, after step 6, the owner had the switch shown ahead of step 7, which still brings the keyboard, reduced motion, light and dark, screen sizes and the budgets up to the quality requirements.
entities.rationale: Changes stay small enough to review, and readers see Cyberspace only when it is whole.
entities.details: The switch was shown on 2026-11-15, after step 6 (pull request 20), ahead of the work this decision had it wait for. Step 7 then brought Cyberspace up to the quality requirements, checked in Chrome on 2026-11-15: keyboard (every part of this repository's component city, every floor of its root tower, every building of its skyline and a part in its street reached and selected from the keyboard alone), reduced motion (every flight, slide, fade and refit at once; walking still moves), light and dark (every scene beside artboards 1 to 6, a change of scheme re-colouring without new geometry, and a contrast test of the labels in test/space.test.js), fallbacks (WebGL off, three.js and dagre blocked, dagre failing on a view, a folder with nothing drawn, a view the models can't build, a lost context restored), screen sizes (every scene at 1280 × 800 to 3440 × 1440), disposal, and the budgets (quality requirement space-frame-rate). With the switch, every row of the spec's Switching modes keeps the place was pressed both ways, and aria-pressed followed the mode; it is hidden on the landing page and without WebGL 2, and stays where three.js couldn't load, so that a later press can work. Safari and Firefox wait for decision cross-browser-checks.

entities.title: Cyberspace: a second way in, in 3D
entities.summary: Beside Flat, the same .dev files can be read as a WebGL scene laid out on the flat drawing's ground plan, drawn with three.js core and the page's own controls and labels.
entities.context: Flat shows a folder's views as drawings, cards and tables. The design canvas Cyberspace explorer in 3D (copied in docs/cyberspace-design/) shows the same views as a tower of floors, a city of glass towers and a street to walk.
entities.decision: Cyberspace is a second way into the same data, never the only one: everything it shows stays readable in Flat, which shows instead wherever Cyberspace can't run. Its ground plan is the flat layout: a part stands where dagre puts its plate on the flat sheet. It is drawn with three.js core only (no OrbitControls, CSS2DRenderer or any other addon, and no post-processing); the camera controls and the labels are the page's own. three.js is pinned to one version and imported from jsDelivr on first entry, as dagre is. An address whose last segment is ~space opens it.
entities.rationale: A reader who switches modes finds everything in the same place. Core three.js is the one new download, and controls and labels written for the page look like the page.
entities.details: Built (plan cyberspace-mode, done 2026-11-15): the address, the Flat / Cyberspace switch (shown in the bar since 2026-11-15) and the fallbacks; four scenes. The folder tower, a folder's .dev files as floors with a drawn view pulled out and its city small on it. The city: a drawn view standing on the flat layout's ground plan, with its labels, legend and camera controls; a tower, plate or beacon can be selected, which lights its beams, opens the inspector on it with the text Flat shows and puts it in the address. The street: eye level by a part, walking with the keys among towers that are solid and plates that are steps, with a map, a breadcrumb and a hover card. The skyline: a repository with several folders as a building per folder, which the reader rises to from a tower and flies into. A city can stand the folder's other drawn views beside it, ticked in its Layers panel, as many as keep the scene within 40 draw calls. Everything works from the keyboard and with reduced motion.

entities.title: The Cyberspace design is copied into the repository
entities.summary: docs/cyberspace-design/ holds the canvas's fifteen artboards and a render of each; the canvas stays the source.
entities.context: The design is a private claude.ai canvas. The agents who build Cyberspace, and anyone reviewing it, can't open it, so the spec's "match the artboard" couldn't be checked.
entities.decision: The artboards (static HTML) and a 1440 × 900 render of each are copied into docs/cyberspace-design/, with a README that says what they show and what they don't. The design changes on the canvas and is copied here again.
entities.rationale: The design can be seen wherever the repository can.
entities.details: There were three artboards when this was decided; the light-mode, skyline and other-kind artboards (4 to 10) joined them on 2026-11-13, and the Gibson look's (11 to 15, decision space-gibson-look) on 2026-11-15, each of those with the image of its scene beside it.

entities.title: What a repository with several folders looks like in Cyberspace
entities.summary: A repository with several folders has a skyline: a scene of its own above the folder towers, as artboard 7 on the canvas draws it.
entities.context: In Cyberspace a folder is a tower of floors. The spec first stood every folder as a building in the tower scene, round the address folder drawn in full, on a radial tree with each subtree's angle in proportion to its number of folders and rings 14 units apart. Drawn for retro-games' 93 folders, that rule stood 15 pairs of buildings closer together than a building is wide, and a full 16 × 12 tower with its drawer did not fit a ring. Artboard 7 (docs/cyberspace-design/Skyline.dc.html) makes the skyline a scene of its own, one level above the towers (~space:skyline): every folder the same building, each subtree given the angle its buildings need, the rings as far apart as that takes (20 units for retro-games), the camera on the address folder with the outer rings running to the horizon. The spec now says the same, so a ~space address still opens a folder's tower.

options.title: Accept artboard 7 and the spec as it now stands
options.consequences: Step 6 builds the skyline as a fourth scene. The tower scene, step 4 and the acceptance checklist's opening stay as they were.

options.title: Keep the skyline inside the tower scene
options.consequences: The address folder's full tower stands among the buildings, which needs wider rings and another layout rule than either the spec's first or the artboard's.

entities.decision: The skyline is as artboard 7 draws it and the spec's sections Skyline world and The skyline say: a scene of its own above the folder towers (~space:skyline), every folder the same building on a radial tree, each subtree given the angle its buildings need, the rings widened until they fit, and the camera on the address folder. A ~space address opens a folder's tower.
entities.rationale: Drawn on retro-games' 93 folders, the artboard's rule leaves no building overlapping another, where the spec's first rule overlapped 15 pairs. The tower scene stays as artboard 1 has it.
entities.details: Built (plan cyberspace-mode, step layers): skylineWorldFrom stands every folder on the radial tree as the decision says; on retro-games' 93 folders of 2026-11-13 (test/fixtures/space/retro-folders.json) the rings are 20 units apart and no two footprints overlap, and this repository's five folders keep 14. buildSkyline draws them in six draw calls with the ground. The scene is ~space:skyline; ~space still opens a folder's tower, and a repository with one folder has no skyline.

entities.title: Cyberspace in light mode
entities.summary: Light mode in Cyberspace is what the page's light tokens give, as artboards 4 to 6 on the canvas draw it.
entities.context: Every colour in Cyberspace comes from the page's tokens (quality requirement light-dark), with four new ones for the sky and the major grid, so light mode follows from the light values. Artboards 4 to 6 (docs/cyberspace-design/StrataLight, MainLight and StreetLight) draw the three scenes from those values. What is lit turns ink-dark, because --hot is the ink colour in light mode: the selected tower's edges, the lit beams, the selected label. Flat's lit lines do the same.

options.title: Accept artboards 4 to 6
options.consequences: Light mode is what the tokens give, and step 7 checks the page against the three artboards.

options.title: Give what is lit its own colour in light mode
options.consequences: A new token beside --hot, which Flat does not have, and artboards 4 to 6 drawn again.

entities.decision: Light mode is what the page's light tokens give, as artboards 4 to 6 draw the three scenes. What is lit is drawn in --hot, the ink colour in light mode, as Flat's lit lines are.
entities.rationale: Cyberspace keeps to the page's tokens and has no colour of its own (quality requirement light-dark), and Flat and Cyberspace light a selection the same way.
entities.details: Superseded by space-gibson-look on 2026-11-15: Cyberspace is always dark, and artboards 4 to 6 are kept as history.

entities.title: How state machines, use cases and parts that open a folder stand in Cyberspace
entities.summary: State machines, use cases and parts that open a folder stand in Cyberspace as artboards 8 to 10 on the canvas draw them.
entities.context: Cyberspace draws every drawn kind as a city. Artboards 8 to 10 (docs/cyberspace-design/StateCity, UseCaseCity and Worker) show this repository's page state machine, its first use case and the Worker. They keep the spec's first defaults for the start point (a disc on the ground), a use case's alternative outcome (a short tower with dashed edges, not a beacon) and a part with diagrams of its own (Flat's badge on its label). They change the rest, and the spec now says the same: a final state is ringed twice and has a solid top, since a second band could not be told from the floor bands; beams between the same two parts fan out; a lit transition shows its trigger; a label is the node's own short label; the Layers panel has a row for each view of a kind; and the inspector shows the folder a part opens, with Enter its folder, in place of Flat's Open link.

options.title: Accept artboards 8 to 10 and the spec as it now stands
Change an artboard
options.consequences: The spec follows the change before the step that builds it.

entities.decision: They stand as artboards 8 to 10 draw them and the spec says: the start point a disc on the ground; a final state ringed twice with a solid top; an alternative outcome a short tower with dashed edges; beams between the same two parts fanned out; a lit transition showing its trigger; labels from the node's own short label; a row in Layers for each view of a kind; and the folder a part opens shown in the inspector, with Enter its folder.
entities.rationale: Each was drawn from this repository's own page state machine, first use case and Worker, where the spec's first defaults could not be told apart or read.
entities.details: Built (plan cyberspace-mode, steps city, selection and layers), and checked in Chrome on 2026-11-15 on this repository's page state machine and component city: the start point a disc, empty the one final state, ringed twice with a solid top; the five transitions between opened and choosing on five arcs; listing's four triggers shown when it is selected; the Worker's label with Flat's badge, and its inspector with the Its folder block and Enter its folder, which opens the Worker's tower.

entities.title: Cyberspace looks like the Gibson in Hackers
entities.summary: Cyberspace is always dark: cyan glass towers whose faces carry their own record, relationships as circuit traces on a black glossy floor that rise as arcs when lit, the kind colour as an accent, as artboards 11 to 15 on the canvas draw it.
entities.context: On 2026-11-15 the owner asked for Cyberspace to look like the Gibson in the film Hackers (1995), from four reference stills: tall translucent cyan-to-teal glass towers densely covered in small glowing monospace text, long straight streets fading into black, a black glossy floor with glowing circuit traces in violet, blue and magenta that turn at right angles and end in pads at the towers' bases, and a black-to-indigo sky. On the stills the owner chose: circuit traces on the floor with arcs only when lit; cyan glass with the kind colour as an accent; tower faces carrying their own data, standing still; and a design pass first. Until then Cyberspace followed the system's colour scheme (decision space-light-mode), drew relationships as arcs of light and its towers as glass in their kind's colour.

options.title: Accept artboards 11 to 15 and the spec as it now stands
options.consequences: Plan cyberspace-gibson builds the look in four pull requests: dark and palette, floor traces, faces, arcs, labels and HUD. Light mode goes from Cyberspace; Flat keeps it.

options.title: Change an artboard first
options.consequences: The spec and the plan follow the change before step G1.

entities.decision: Cyberspace is always dark: while it shows, the whole window takes the page's dark tokens, and Cyberspace's own tokens colour the scene and its panels; Flat keeps its own theme (the system's setting, and since 2026-11-18 the bar's theme switch, decision theme-switch). Towers are cyan-to-teal glass; the kind colour accents their edges, pads, labels, plates and the frames on their faces. Each tower's faces carry its own record as the inspector shows it, in glowing monospace: its name, kind, description and file on two faces, its relationships on the other two; a short record repeats down its face, dimmed, and a long one is cut with an ellipsis; at a distance the text thins into a haze; nothing moves unless the camera does. Every relationship is a glowing circuit trace on the floor, routed at right angles along the streets dagre's own route takes, between pins on the two parts' pads, parallel traces in lanes; a selected part's relationships also rise as arcs of light, and the quiet arcs go. Beacons are magenta, as are the traces that reach them. The glows are geometry with a falloff in its own shader: no post-processing, three.js core only.
entities.rationale: It is the look the owner chose, and a prototype drawn from this repository's data with three.js core alone shows it holds the budgets: 9 draw calls for a city of any size (10 with a selection), 7 for the skyline, and frames of 1.5 to 3.6 ms on an M1 Pro at up to 3440 × 1440 and device pixel ratio 2, without multisampling at that pixel ratio. Every word on a face is the part's own, and every relationship stays on the floor whether or not anything is selected.

origin.description: Make Cyberspace always dark, styled like the Gibson in Hackers; selecting something should turn the view toward it.

entities.details:
The owner accepted artboards 11 to 15 on 2026-11-15, after asking for thinner lines at the buildings' edges. Measured in the scratch prototype that drew artboards 11 to 15 (2026-11-15, M1 Pro, Chrome for Testing): the face atlas is 512 × 1024 RGBA (2.7 MiB with its mips), built in 33 to 53 ms; a city's face text is 2 bytes a cell (47 KB for this repository's component city, 381 KB for the 400 parts of perf/400-parts); routing 474 traces takes 31 ms; no trace of this repository's 20 drawn views, retro-games' 142 or the 400-part city passes through a tower. Frame times are in the spec's Performance budgets, measured with a pixel read back: gl.finish() returned before the GPU had finished there. In the page, after step G1 (the dark, the palette, the sky, the floor, the glass and the glowing edges, without traces, faces or reflections yet), the same machine measured frames of 2.9 to 7.8 ms on average with a pixel read back, at 1440 × 900 and 3440 × 1440 and device pixel ratio 2: 1.9 to 3.6 times the prototype's, because the page's frame also places the labels, which the prototype's didn't; still within the budgets (quality requirement space-frame-rate). A city draws in 9 calls there with nothing selected, as in the prototype, and the skyline in 7. In the page, after step G3 (the faces, the floors' and buildings' text, the reflections; 2026-11-18): the atlas is the prototype's size and takes 34 ms the first time a stage draws it and about 10 ms after, against the prototype's 33 to 53; it holds 218 glyphs, not 205, since the repositories' records use arrows, mathematical signs and ⌘; this repository's component city is 24,740 cells (51 KB) and the 400-part city 195,466 (382 KB), the repository having grown since; laying out the 400-part city's faces takes 12.1 ms, reading each part's inspector HTML among it, against the prototype's 4.7 for faceText alone. A city drew in 9 calls with nothing selected, as in the prototype, and in 11 with a part selected until step G4 made the lit beams arcs; the skyline in 7. Walking by Loader at 3440 × 1440 and device pixel ratio 2 stood at its 8 ms target on an M1 Pro, the face text costing 1.2 to 1.5 ms of it, where the prototype put the face text at 0.1 ms of a frame that placed no labels.

Built: plan cyberspace-gibson, done on 2026-11-19 in four pull requests (G1 #25, G2 #26, G3 #29 and G4). Since G4 a city draws in 9 calls and 10 with a part selected, as in the prototype, and the scene keeps 3 of its 40 for the sky, the floor and the arcs. Where what was built differs from what was decided, each said in the spec's section The Gibson look: G1 kept the first look's pill shape, 22 px with a radius of 4, which the artboards draw too, so G4 changed only the labels' rules and words; G2's router departs from the first rule in four places (its stubs, its streets, the pads it keeps clear of, and the fallback grid's Zs), each for a view of the two repositories where the first rule put a trace through a tower or two traces in one lane; G3's glyph set is 218, not 205, because the repositories' records use arrows, mathematical signs and ⌘, and its reflections draw the towers' back faces, because mirroring turns the triangles' winding; between G2 and G3 the owner ruled that Cyberspace stays dark whatever Flat's new theme switch says (decision theme-switch); G4 does not mirror the arcs (the stills' arcs rise over the floor alone, and a third reflection would take a selection to 11 calls), keeps a dashed relationship's arc as every other segment, as its tube was, measures the street's 18 units from the eye to the label's anchor (the prototype took the depth along the view), fits a city stood from an address to the arcs of the part it names, and folds the legend's badge, then all its words, into icons where they would run past the window's right edge less 20 px (with the arc and the badge, this repository's component legend is 1,095 px wide).

entities.title: Use cases and journeys side by side in Cyberspace
entities.summary: A file of several use cases becomes one city per use case. Whether readers can stand them side by side is decided after step 6.
entities.context: Flat draws one canvas per use case or journey, and the spec builds one city per entity, chosen in the address. Standing several side by side would be the Layers mechanism of step 6 applied to entities. What steps 6 and 7 found: cities side by side need no new rules, since every city is placed by its bounds and picked, labelled and walked by its view and part; but each is its own meshes, and the 40-call cap the Layers panel keeps lets about four to six cities stand at once.

entities.title: Who checks Cyberspace in Safari and Firefox
entities.summary: The acceptance checklist runs in Chrome, Safari and Firefox, and only Chrome can be driven by an agent on the machine the work is checked on.
entities.context: That machine has Chrome for Testing, but no WebKit or Firefox build an agent can drive.

options.title: The owner runs the checklist in Safari and Firefox
options.consequences: Nothing to download; the owner's time, once and after changes to Cyberspace.

options.title: Install Playwright's WebKit and Firefox builds
options.consequences: About 200 MB downloaded once; an agent runs the checklist in all three.

entities.title: A light and dark switch for Flat; Cyberspace stays dark
entities.summary: The bar has a System / Light / Dark switch, kept in the browser, which picks Flat's theme. Cyberspace is always dark whatever it says, and the switch is disabled while Cyberspace shows.
entities.context: Flat followed the system's colour scheme with no way to choose (limitation system-theme-only), and Cyberspace was always dark (decision space-gibson-look). On 2026-11-18 the owner asked for the explorer to fully support dark and light mode, and for a VS Code extension, which has to follow the editor's theme. Pull request #27 (merged 2026-11-18) built the switch for Flat and Cyberspace both: every --space-* token got a light value, glows were laid over a pale floor by day, and a MutationObserver on data-theme repainted Cyberspace in place. The same day the owner ruled that Cyberspace stays always dark, which amends the decision as #27 merged it: the switch is Flat's alone.
entities.decision: html[data-theme] is light or dark and picks Flat's token block: the light :root, or the dark block, which is written once under :root[data-theme="dark"], :root.space. The bar's switch sets it: System follows prefers-color-scheme, live; Light and Dark are kept in localStorage under cyberspace-explorer:theme, read by a script in the head before the first paint. A host that marks html data-theme-host (the VS Code extension) owns the attribute, and the switch hides. Cyberspace is always dark, by the owner's ruling of 2026-11-18 (decision space-gibson-look): while it shows, html.space takes the dark block whatever html[data-theme] says, Cyberspace's own tokens have only their dark value, and nothing in Cyberspace listens to the theme. The switch stays in the bar while Cyberspace shows, its buttons disabled with the title "Cyberspace is always dark: the theme is Flat's", and leaving Cyberspace enables them again. A choice made in another tab, or a change of the system's setting, while Cyberspace shows still sets html[data-theme], and Flat shows it on return.
entities.rationale: A reader chooses what suits their room and screen for Flat, and a host can match its own theme; Cyberspace stays the Gibson by night that the owner chose, one look to keep and to measure.

origin.description: Make the cyberspace explorer fully support dark and light mode, then create a VS Code extension for it.

options.title: Flat and Cyberspace both follow the switch (as pull request #27 built it)
options.consequences: Cyberspace gets a day look of its own, a light value for every --space-* token, glows laid over the floor by day, and repaints in place on a change.

options.title: The switch is Flat's; Cyberspace stays always dark
options.consequences: Cyberspace keeps the Gibson look of decision space-gibson-look and its tokens one value each; the switch rests while Cyberspace shows.

entities.details: As pull request #27 merged it (2026-11-18, merge 4daa9af), Cyberspace followed the switch too, with a light value for every --space-* token, retheme and stage.repaint, and the floor's traces blended by MinEquation by day. The owner's ruling of the same day undid that for Cyberspace only: its rendering is step G2's again (merge c51a6b5), and the switch, the head script, html[data-theme] and its two token blocks, the VS Code extension and its workspace source, --error and --verified stay.

entities.title: A VS Code extension that hosts the page
entities.summary: The extension in vscode/ shows index.html itself in a webview, reading the workspace folder's files through a local source, rather than a second implementation.
entities.context: The owner asked for a VS Code extension for the explorer on 2026-11-18. The page reads repositories from GitHub and GitLab; in the editor the views are on disk, often uncommitted.
entities.decision: vscode/ holds a plain-JavaScript extension with no build. It reads index.html (copied into media/ when packaged), adds a content security policy and a nonce to every script, and puts a first script before the page's that hands it window.cyberspaceWorkspace (the folder's view paths and a webview URL to fetch them under), the theme from VS Code's colour theme, and the address it was at. The page's local source lists and reads those, with no token and no ?url=. Paths in the page open files in the editor through a command link. The panel reloads when a view file changes and comes back after a restart.
entities.rationale: One page to maintain: everything the website gains, the extension gains, and decision one-file holds.

entities.title: A dock, diagrams over the scene, and a warp between places
entities.summary: Cyberspace has a dock at the left edge: Back, Forward, History, a bookmark and the bookmarks, and a button per kind of drawn view. A kind's view is drawn in neon over the blurred scene, and its parts lead there through a turn, an afterglow, a warp and a moment of darkness.
entities.context: The owner asked for this on 2026-11-19: a left sidebar with buttons for the diagram types; tapping one blurs the screen and overlays the diagram in neon; tapping a node that navigates shows the blurred scene turn to face the target, the diagram goes out leaving a little afterglow, the blur becomes a warp as the reader flies there at breakneck speed, and the warp ends with the screen opaque for a moment, except the HUD, fading to the cityscape. Also back and forward buttons, a history and bookmarks, as in a browser.

options.title: Build it on the address
options.consequences: Every arrival is a new history entry, so the browser's Back and Forward are the dock's; history and bookmarks keep addresses. Nothing new to keep in step.

options.title: A navigation stack of its own
options.consequences: Could remember camera poses, at the cost of a second source of truth beside the address.

entities.decision: Built on the address (decision address-is-state). The diagram is Flat's own drawing (sheetOf, drawSvg) restyled; a part that opens a folder leads to its tower, any other to itself in its view's city. With reduced motion there is no turn, warp or darkness: the address changes at once. The warp is motion the reader asked for, so it stays within cyberspace-motion. History and bookmarks are kept in this browser (localStorage), places as their address and hash. 'Leaving cyberspace' in the owner's words is read as leaving the warp, since what follows is the cityscape.

entities.title: What a use case touches is inferred, and says so
entities.summary: A use case or journey brought over a city lights the parts its steps seem to touch, matched from the sources each step cites and its words, and the diagram's note says the match is inferred.
entities.context: The owner asked that constructs such as use cases highlight the things they affect. No field in describe-use-case links a step to a part of another view: a step has an actor, an action and sources, and relatedViews names whole files.

options.title: Infer, and say so
options.consequences: Works on every repository today; can light too much or too little.

options.title: Add a field to the skill upstream
options.consequences: Exact, but every repository's use cases would need it written (backlog step-touches).

entities.decision: Infer, and say so: a part counts when a step's source lies in its folder (not the root), or a step's source symbol or words name it or its id as whole words of three letters or more (affectedBy). Hovering a step lights only its own matches.
